name: PHA (polyhydroxy acid)

lead: Polyhydroxy acids are acids with several hydroxyl groups, used in skincare as exfoliants and humectants. The best-known are gluconolactone and lactobionic acid.
They are marketed as lower-irritation alternatives to glycolic acid for sensitive skin. Evidence consists of a few small comparisons and safety assessments rather than large trials.

paras: Their larger molecular size is said to slow penetration, and their many hydroxyl groups bind water and metal ions, giving moisturising and antioxidant behaviour alongside mild exfoliation.
Described as well tolerated. Regulators say AHAs in general can raise sunburn likelihood, and sun protection is commonly advised on labels.

lead: Polyhydroxy acids (PHAs) are a group of organic acids that carry multiple hydroxyl groups and are used in cosmetics as mild exfoliants and humectants. The two usually named are gluconolactone and lactobionic acid.[1][2] Gluconolactone is the lactone of gluconic acid, an oxidised derivative of glucose, and lactobionic acid is a gluconic acid-galactose disaccharide.[2][3]

Marketing positions PHAs as lower-irritation alternatives to alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic acid. A summary of the small trial literature reports similar performance to AHAs in some measures with less stinging in some comparisons.[1] No larger independent trials were found.

paras: Gluconolactone is used both as the food additive E575 and in leave-on and rinse-off cosmetics.[1][2] Lactobionic acid is made by oxidising lactose and is used in organ-preservation solutions and cosmetics.[3]

No class-level clinical trials were found. For gluconolactone specifically, Grokipedia summarises small comparisons with glycolic acid and benzoyl peroxide, including one 150-patient acne trial, reporting fewer side effects with gluconolactone.[1] These summaries have not been independently checked against the original papers.

The Cosmetic Ingredient Review is reported to have found gluconolactone safe at current use levels.[1] For the AHA class, the FDA and CIR have said safety depends on low concentration, pH above 3.5 and safety instructions, with mild irritation common and increased sunburn likelihood that reverses on stopping.[4]
